title: Product Management Foundations
description: Learn what a product manager does and how an idea becomes a shipped product that solves a real user problem.

lessons.title: The product manager's job
lessons.goal: Explain what a product manager owns and how they work with design and engineering.

slides.html:
LESSON 1 · THE ROLE

The product manager's job

A team can build almost anything. Someone has to decide what is worth building, and why.
slides.narration: A team of designers and engineers can build almost anything. So who decides what is actually worth building, and for whom? In this lesson you meet the product manager, often shortened to PM, the person who owns that question.

slides.html:
THE IDEA

A PM owns the why and the what

Product manager
Why build it? What should we build?
Design
How should it look and feel?
Engineering
How do we build it?
The PM leads by being clear and persuasive. A PM is not the boss of the team.
slides.narration: A product manager owns the why and the what. Why means the problem we solve and the goal. What means which solution we choose to build. Designers shape how it looks and feels, and engineers decide how it is built. The PM is a teammate, not their boss.

slides.html:
EXAMPLE

A meal-planning app

PM: People give up planning their week. Let's build a weekly meal plan.
Engineer: A shopping list is quick. Importing photos takes weeks.
PM: Then we ship the plan and the list first.
slides.narration: Say the app helps people plan meals. The PM sees that people give up planning their week, and proposes a weekly meal plan. An engineer explains that a shopping list is quick, but importing photos takes weeks. Together they agree to ship the plan and the list first.

slides.html:
REMEMBER

Two things to keep

1. The PM owns the why and the what.
2. Design and engineering own the how. The PM works with them, and is not their boss.
slides.narration: To remember: first, a product manager owns the why and the what of a product. Second, designers and engineers own the how, and the PM works with them as a partner who explains the goal and listens, rather than giving orders.

test.prompt: Which pair of questions does a product manager mainly own?
choices: How is the code organised, and which tools do we use?
How should it look, and which colours do we pick?
Why are we building this, and what should we build?
Who works on what, and who gets promoted?
test.explanation: The PM owns the why (the problem and goal) and the what (the solution to build). How the code is organised and how it looks belong to engineering and design.

test.prompt: An engineer says a feature will take six weeks. What should a good PM do?
choices: Talk through the trade-offs together and adjust the scope or plan
Order the engineer to finish it in two weeks
Overrule the estimate, since the PM decides how it is built
Accept it silently and stop asking questions
test.explanation: A PM works with engineering, not above them. Discussing trade-offs and trimming scope keeps the goal. Ordering or overruling treats the PM as the boss, which the role is not.

variants.prompt: A team is debating a new feature. Which decision belongs mainly to the product manager?
choices: Who works on what, and who gets promoted?
Why are we building this, and what should we build?
How should it look, and which colours do we pick?
How is the code organised, and which tools do we use?
variants.explanation: The PM owns what to build and why, so deciding which problem to solve first is the PM's call. The code structure and the visual style are decided by engineering and design.

variants.prompt: Imagine you are the PM. Which two questions should you be able to answer about your product?
choices: How should it look, and which colours do we pick?
Why are we building this, and what should we build?
Who works on what, and who gets promoted?
How is the code organised, and which tools do we use?
variants.explanation: A PM should be able to explain why the product exists and what it should do. Code structure, colours and staffing are not the core of the role.

variants.prompt: The design is ready, but engineers warn it needs far more time than planned. What is the best PM response?
choices: Accept it silently and stop asking questions
Overrule the estimate, since the PM decides how it is built
Order the engineer to finish it in two weeks
Talk through the trade-offs together and adjust the scope or plan
variants.explanation: The PM should work with the team on trade-offs and scope. Pushing for a deadline or overruling the estimate treats the PM as the boss.

variants.prompt: Your team tells you one part of the plan is very costly to build. How do you respond as PM?
choices: Order the engineer to finish it in two weeks
Overrule the estimate, since the PM decides how it is built
Accept it silently and stop asking questions
Talk through the trade-offs together and adjust the scope or plan
variants.explanation: A good PM discusses options with the team and adapts the scope. The PM owns the what and why, not how it is built.

lessons.title: Users and problems
lessons.goal: Describe a user problem in one clear sentence before thinking about any solution.

slides.html:
LESSON 2 · THE START

Users and problems

People do not want a new button. They want something to stop being hard.
slides.narration: People rarely want a new button or a new screen. What they want is for something in their life to stop being slow, confusing or frustrating. Good product work starts from that frustration, which we call the user problem.

slides.html:
THE IDEA

Problem first, solution second

Solution
An idea for what to build. Example: add a chat button.
Problem
Something hard for a specific person.
Frame it: [User] struggles to [do something] because [reason].
slides.narration: A solution is an idea for what to build, like a chat button. A problem is something that is hard for a specific person. Start with the problem. Then frame it in one sentence: this user struggles to do something because of this reason.

slides.html:
EXAMPLE

From idea to problem

Idea: add dark mode. Ask: who needs it, and why?
Night readers struggle to read comfortably in bed because the screen is too bright.
Now dark mode, a warmer tint or a dimmer screen are all possible solutions.
slides.narration: Suppose someone suggests adding dark mode. Ask who needs it and why. You might find that night readers struggle to read comfortably in bed because the screen is too bright. Now dark mode is only one of several solutions, so the team can pick the best one.

slides.html:
REMEMBER

Two things to keep

1. Start with a user problem, not a solution.
2. Frame it: a user struggles to do something because of a reason.
slides.narration: To remember: start with a user problem, not a solution. A problem is something hard for a specific person. Then write it in one sentence: this user struggles to do something because of this reason. Only after that should you compare solutions.

test.prompt: Which of these is a user problem rather than a solution?
choices: Add a voice-note button to the app
New parents struggle to find a quiet moment to log their baby's feeds
Send a weekly email digest to every user
Redesign the home screen with four tabs
test.explanation: A problem describes something hard for a person. The other three are ideas for what to build, so they are solutions, not problems.

test.prompt: Which sentence frames a problem with a user, a struggle and a reason?
choices: Commuters struggle to buy tickets because the queue at the machine is long
Commuters need a ticket app with a QR code
The ticket machines are old and should be replaced
We want to sell more tickets this year
test.explanation: The first sentence names who, what is hard, and why. The others state a solution, an internal opinion or a business wish, not the user's struggle.

variants.prompt: A teammate brings the team four statements. Which one describes a problem and not a solution?
choices: Redesign the home screen with four tabs
Send a weekly email digest to every user
New parents struggle to find a quiet moment to log their baby's feeds
Add a voice-note button to the app
variants.explanation: Only one statement describes a difficulty a person has. Buttons, emails and redesigns are things we could build in response.

variants.prompt: Which statement describes what is hard for a user, without proposing what to build?
choices: New parents struggle to find a quiet moment to log their baby's feeds
Send a weekly email digest to every user
Redesign the home screen with four tabs
Add a voice-note button to the app
variants.explanation: A problem names the struggle. A new button, a digest and a redesign are all solutions to something not yet named.

variants.prompt: You want to write a problem in the form user, struggle, reason. Which sentence does that?
choices: We want to sell more tickets this year
The ticket machines are old and should be replaced
Commuters need a ticket app with a QR code
Commuters struggle to buy tickets because the queue at the machine is long
variants.explanation: Only one sentence has a user, something they struggle to do, and a reason. The rest are solutions or business goals.

variants.prompt: Pick the best one-sentence problem frame for a team working on a library app.
choices: Commuters need a ticket app with a QR code
The ticket machines are old and should be replaced
We want to sell more tickets this year
Commuters struggle to buy tickets because the queue at the machine is long
variants.explanation: A good frame names who struggles, with what, and why. Solutions and company wishes do not name the user's difficulty.

lessons.title: Outcomes, not outputs
lessons.goal: Tell an output from an outcome and judge a release by the change it causes.

slides.html:
LESSON 3 · THE GOAL

Outcomes, not outputs

You shipped it. Did anything change?
slides.narration: Your team worked hard and shipped the feature on time. Great. But did anything change for your users, or for the business? That question is the difference between an output and an outcome, and good product managers care most about the second.

slides.html:
THE IDEA

Output versus outcome

Output
What the team makes and ships: a feature, a page, a release.
Outcome
A change in what users do, or in the business result.
The output is the means. The outcome is the point.
slides.narration: An output is what the team makes and ships, like a feature, a page or a release. An outcome is the change that results, either in what users do or in a business result. The output is only the means. The outcome is the point.

slides.html:
EXAMPLE

A save-for-later button

Output: the button ships on time.
Outcome we wanted: more readers come back to finish articles.
Result: many taps, few returns. Output delivered, outcome not yet. Time to learn why.
slides.narration: A team ships a save for later button. That is the output. The outcome they wanted was more readers coming back to finish articles. After launch the button is tapped a lot, but few readers return. The output was delivered, the outcome was not, so the team investigates why.

slides.html:
REMEMBER

Two things to keep

1. Output = what we ship. Outcome = the change it causes.
2. Judge a release by its outcome, not by shipping on time.
slides.narration: To remember: an output is what you ship, and an outcome is the change it causes in user behaviour or business results. Judge a release by its outcome. Shipping on time is good, but it only counts as success if something changed.

test.prompt: Which of these is an outcome rather than an output?
choices: We launched the new onboarding screens
The team closed twelve tickets this sprint
Search now supports filters
More new users finish their first lesson
test.explanation: An outcome is a change in what users do. Screens, closed tickets and a new filter are things the team made, so they are outputs.

test.prompt: A feature ships on schedule, but user behaviour does not change. What is the fairest conclusion?
choices: It was a success because it shipped on time
The output was delivered, but the outcome is not achieved yet, so learn why
The users are wrong, so no changes are needed
The engineers failed because they missed the output
test.explanation: Shipping on time delivers the output, not the outcome. Blaming users or engineers skips the useful step: find out why behaviour did not change.

variants.prompt: A manager lists results from last month. Which one is an outcome?
choices: More new users finish their first lesson
Search now supports filters
The team closed twelve tickets this sprint
We launched the new onboarding screens
variants.explanation: Only one item describes a change in user behaviour. The rest describe work the team delivered.

variants.prompt: Which statement reports a change for users instead of work the team finished?
choices: The team closed twelve tickets this sprint
Search now supports filters
More new users finish their first lesson
We launched the new onboarding screens
variants.explanation: An outcome is what changes because of the work. Launches, closed tickets and filters are the work itself.

variants.prompt: Your team launched a release on the planned date, yet people use the product exactly as before. How should you judge it?
choices: The engineers failed because they missed the output
The users are wrong, so no changes are needed
The output was delivered, but the outcome is not achieved yet, so learn why
It was a success because it shipped on time
variants.explanation: The output is done, but the intended change did not happen. The right move is to learn why, not to call it a success or blame someone.

variants.prompt: After launch, nothing changes in how people behave. What should the PM conclude?
choices: The output was delivered, but the outcome is not achieved yet, so learn why
The users are wrong, so no changes are needed
The engineers failed because they missed the output
It was a success because it shipped on time
variants.explanation: On-time delivery is only the output. Without a behaviour change the outcome has not been reached, so investigate.

lessons.title: Choosing what to build first
lessons.goal: Rank a short list of ideas by impact and effort and pick the first one.

slides.html:
LESSON 4 · PRIORITISING

Choosing what to build first

You have ten good ideas and time for one. Which goes first?
slides.narration: Every team has more ideas than time. Choosing which one to build first is called prioritising. A simple way to start is to compare each idea on two things: how much good it does, and how much work it takes.

slides.html:
THE IDEA

Impact versus effort

Impact
How much it helps users or the goal.
Effort
How much time and work it costs.
Start with high impact, low effort. Put low impact, high effort last.
slides.narration: Impact is how much an idea helps your users or your goal. Effort is how much time and work it costs to build. Start with ideas that have high impact and low effort, since they give the most value for the least cost. Low impact and high effort goes last.

slides.html:
EXAMPLE

A class-booking app

Class reminderImpact High, effort Low
Fix slow payment pageImpact High, effort Medium
Dark modeImpact Low, effort Low
Redesign whole appImpact Medium, effort High
Order: reminder, payment fix, dark mode, redesign.
slides.narration: Here are four ideas for a class booking app. A class reminder is high impact and low effort, so it goes first. Fixing the slow payment page is high impact with medium effort, so it comes second. Dark mode is cheap but small, and the full redesign comes last.

slides.html:
REMEMBER

Two things to keep

1. Rank ideas by impact and effort, and start with high impact, low effort.
2. The scores are rough estimates. Set them with engineers and update them as you learn.
slides.narration: To remember: rank ideas by impact and effort, and start with high impact and low effort. The high, medium and low scores are rough estimates, not facts. Agree them with your engineers and update them as the team learns more.

test.prompt: When comparing ideas by impact and effort, which kind is usually the best to start with?
choices: High impact and low effort, since it gives the most value for the least cost
High impact and high effort, since big ideas matter most
Low impact and low effort, since it is the safest choice
Low impact and high effort, since the team learns the most
test.explanation: High impact with low effort gives the most value per unit of work. Big costly ideas may still be worth it later, but they are not the natural first pick.

test.prompt: Idea X has high impact and low effort. Idea Y has low impact and high effort. Idea Z has medium impact and medium effort. Which order is best?
choices: Y, then Z, then X
Z, then X, then Y
X, then Z, then Y
X, then Y, then Z
test.explanation: X gives the most value for the least work, Y gives the least value for the most work, and Z sits in between. Putting Y second or first wastes the team's time.

test.prompt: Where should the high, medium and low scores come from?
choices: Exact measurements taken from the finished feature
Rough team estimates, agreed with engineering and updated as you learn
The PM's own gut feeling, without asking engineers
A formula that gives the one right answer
test.explanation: Scores are estimates made before building, so they are rough and can change. Engineers help judge effort, and no formula gives a certain answer.

variants.prompt: You must pick one idea from a list scored on impact and effort. Which kind is the usual first choice?
choices: Low impact and high effort, since the team learns the most
Low impact and low effort, since it is the safest choice
High impact and high effort, since big ideas matter most
High impact and low effort, since it gives the most value for the least cost
variants.explanation: Value for cost is the point of this method, so high impact and low effort comes first.

variants.prompt: Which combination should the team normally build first when using impact and effort?
choices: High impact and high effort, since big ideas matter most
Low impact and low effort, since it is the safest choice
Low impact and high effort, since the team learns the most
High impact and low effort, since it gives the most value for the least cost
variants.explanation: High impact for low effort gives the best return. High effort ideas and low impact ideas wait.

variants.prompt: Three ideas: A is high impact and low effort, B is medium on both, C is low impact and high effort. How should you order them?
choices: X, then Y, then Z
X, then Z, then Y
Z, then X, then Y
Y, then Z, then X
variants.explanation: Rank from best value for cost to worst. The order is A, then B, then C.

variants.prompt: A list has one cheap, valuable idea, one middle idea and one costly, small idea. Which order do you build in?
choices: Z, then X, then Y
X, then Z, then Y
X, then Y, then Z
Y, then Z, then X
variants.explanation: Start with the cheap and valuable one, then the middle one, and leave the costly and small one last.

variants.prompt: A teammate says the impact and effort scores are exact facts. What is the best response?
choices: A formula that gives the one right answer
The PM's own gut feeling, without asking engineers
Rough team estimates, agreed with engineering and updated as you learn
Exact measurements taken from the finished feature
variants.explanation: The scores are rough estimates made with the team, and they should be updated when you learn more.

variants.prompt: How should a PM set effort scores for the ideas on a list?
choices: Rough team estimates, agreed with engineering and updated as you learn
The PM's own gut feeling, without asking engineers
A formula that gives the one right answer
Exact measurements taken from the finished feature
variants.explanation: Ask engineers and agree on rough estimates. Gut feeling alone, exact measures and a perfect formula are not available before building.

lessons.title: Writing a clear problem statement
lessons.goal: Write a short problem statement with who, the problem, why it matters and how we will know.

slides.html:
LESSON 5 · WRITING

Writing a clear problem statement

If the team reads your idea and pictures different things, the idea is not clear yet.
slides.narration: Once you have chosen an idea, the team needs to read the same thing and picture the same thing. A short problem statement does that. It is a few sentences that say what problem we are solving, for whom, and how we will know it worked.

slides.html:
THE IDEA

Four parts

1. Who
The user
2. Problem
What is hard
3. Why it matters
The cost of leaving it
4. How we will know
The change we expect to see
slides.narration: A clear problem statement has four parts. First, who has the problem. Second, what the problem is. Third, why it matters, meaning what it costs the user or the business. Fourth, how we will know it is solved, meaning what change we expect to see.

slides.html:
EXAMPLE

A library app

Who: Parents of young children.
Problem: They forget to return books before the due date.
Why: Fines build up and they stop borrowing.
Know: Fewer late returns, and more parents keep borrowing.
slides.narration: Here is an example for a library app. Who: parents of young children. Problem: they forget to return books before the due date. Why it matters: fines build up and they stop borrowing. How we will know: fewer late returns, and more parents keep borrowing.

slides.html:
REMEMBER

Two things to keep

1. Four parts: who, problem, why it matters, how we will know.
2. Describe the problem, not the solution.
slides.narration: To remember: a problem statement has four parts, which are who, the problem, why it matters, and how we will know. And keep it about the problem. If your statement says build an app, it has jumped to a solution too early.

test.prompt: Which list names the four parts of a clear problem statement?
choices: Who, the solution, the deadline, the budget
The problem, the feature, the design, the launch date
Who, the problem, the team, the tools
Who, the problem, why it matters, how we will know
test.explanation: A problem statement names the user, the problem, its cost, and the sign of success. Solutions, dates, budgets and tools belong to later planning.

test.prompt: Which statement names a solution instead of a problem?
choices: Build a reminder app so people remember to water plants
Home gardeners forget to water plants, so many plants die
Beginner gardeners lose plants they paid for and give up the hobby
Plant owners struggle to know when each plant needs water
test.explanation: The first sentence says what to build. The others describe who struggles and why, which is what a problem statement should do.

variants.prompt: You are asked to write a problem statement. Which four things should it contain?
choices: Who, the problem, why it matters, how we will know
Who, the problem, the team, the tools
The problem, the feature, the design, the launch date
Who, the solution, the deadline, the budget
variants.explanation: The four parts are who, the problem, why it matters and how we will know. Deadlines, features and tools come later.

variants.prompt: A teammate lists what a problem statement needs. Which list is correct?
choices: The problem, the feature, the design, the launch date
Who, the problem, the team, the tools
Who, the problem, why it matters, how we will know
Who, the solution, the deadline, the budget
variants.explanation: A statement needs the user, the problem, why it matters and a sign of success. The other lists mix in solutions, plans or resources.

variants.prompt: Which of these sentences jumps straight to something to build?
choices: Plant owners struggle to know when each plant needs water
Beginner gardeners lose plants they paid for and give up the hobby
Home gardeners forget to water plants, so many plants die
Build a reminder app so people remember to water plants
variants.explanation: A sentence that says build or add something is a solution. The others describe a user's difficulty.

variants.prompt: A teammate wrote four lines for a plant-care project. Which one is a solution, not a problem?
choices: Home gardeners forget to water plants, so many plants die
Beginner gardeners lose plants they paid for and give up the hobby
Plant owners struggle to know when each plant needs water
Build a reminder app so people remember to water plants
variants.explanation: Only one line proposes something to build. The remaining three describe the people and what is hard for them.

lessons.title: Measuring success
lessons.goal: Define one success metric with a guardrail, a target and a time window.

slides.html:
LESSON 6 · MEASURING

Measuring success

How will you know it worked? Decide before you build.
slides.narration: Before the team builds anything, decide how you will know it worked. Otherwise every result can be argued as a win. A good plan uses a small number of clear measures, with a target and a deadline for each.

slides.html:
THE IDEA

Metric, guardrail, target, window

Success metric
One number showing the outcome you want.
Guardrail
A number that must not get worse.
Add a target and a time window: from this level to that level, by this date.
slides.narration: Pick one success metric, the number that shows the outcome you want. Add one guardrail metric, a number that must not get worse while you chase the first. Then set a target and a time window, meaning from what level to what level, and by when.

slides.html:
EXAMPLE

A faster checkout

Success: share who finish checkout, 60% to 70% in eight weeks (example numbers).
Guardrail: refund requests do not rise.
Leading (early signal): people reaching the payment step this week. Lagging (final result): orders completed over the quarter.
slides.narration: Take an online shop that wants a faster checkout. The success metric is the share of people who finish checkout. An example target is sixty to seventy percent within eight weeks. The guardrail is that refund requests must not rise. A leading metric moves early, like reaching the payment step. A lagging one, like completed orders, shows the result later.

slides.html:
REMEMBER

Two things to keep

1. One success metric, one guardrail, with a target and a time window.
2. Leading metrics move early. Lagging metrics show the final result later.
slides.narration: To remember: choose one success metric and one guardrail, then set a target and a time window. And use both kinds of signals. Leading metrics move early so you can react quickly, while lagging metrics show whether the real result arrived.

test.prompt: What is a guardrail metric for?
choices: Measuring the same success a second time to be sure
Checking that chasing the success metric does not harm something important
Setting the deadline for the project
Counting how many features the team shipped
test.explanation: A guardrail protects something else you care about, such as refunds or complaints, while you push the success metric. It is not a second copy of success or a deadline.

test.prompt: Which goal has both a clear target and a time window?
choices: Raise checkout completion from 60% to 70% within eight weeks of launch
Make checkout much better soon
Raise checkout completion as high as possible
Keep improving checkout completion over time
test.explanation: A target says from what level to what level, and the window says by when. The other goals are vague, so no one can tell whether they were met.

test.prompt: A team launches a new onboarding. Which measure is the leading one?
choices: Share of new users still active three months later
Total revenue earned this year
Share of new users who finish the first lesson on day one
Number of onboarding screens the team built
test.explanation: A leading metric moves early and hints at the final result. Still active in three months and yearly revenue are lagging, and screens built is an output, not a measure of user behaviour.

variants.prompt: A team pushes hard to raise sign-ups. Why would they also track a guardrail metric?
choices: Counting how many features the team shipped
Setting the deadline for the project
Checking that chasing the success metric does not harm something important
Measuring the same success a second time to be sure
variants.explanation: To make sure the push does not damage something else, such as quality or complaints.

variants.prompt: Which describes the job of a guardrail metric?
choices: Checking that chasing the success metric does not harm something important
Setting the deadline for the project
Counting how many features the team shipped
Measuring the same success a second time to be sure
variants.explanation: A guardrail watches for harm elsewhere while you improve the main number. It does not repeat success, set dates or count features.

variants.prompt: Which goal could you check clearly at the end of a quarter?
choices: Keep improving checkout completion over time
Raise checkout completion as high as possible
Make checkout much better soon
Raise checkout completion from 60% to 70% within eight weeks of launch
variants.explanation: Only a goal with a starting level, a target level and a deadline can be checked. Vague goals like soon, as high as possible or over time cannot.

variants.prompt: A teammate proposes four goals for a new feature. Which one is measurable with a deadline?
choices: Make checkout much better soon
Raise checkout completion as high as possible
Keep improving checkout completion over time
Raise checkout completion from 60% to 70% within eight weeks of launch
variants.explanation: The measurable goal names a target and a time window. The others leave both open.

variants.prompt: You want an early sign that a new sign-up flow works. Which measure moves first?
choices: Number of onboarding screens the team built
Share of new users who finish the first lesson on day one
Total revenue earned this year
Share of new users still active three months later
variants.explanation: An early measure moves soon after launch and hints at the final result. Later retention and yearly revenue are lagging, and screens built is an output.

variants.prompt: Which of these would you check in the first days after launch to predict success?
choices: Total revenue earned this year
Share of new users who finish the first lesson on day one
Number of onboarding screens the team built
Share of new users still active three months later
variants.explanation: A leading metric appears quickly. The others either take months to show or measure the team's work, not user behaviour.
